passage:
Tuesday, late. Ma's scan results come on Thursday and I have been pacing the flat since six. So I took the back of an envelope and made two lists. Things I can do: book the driver for Thursday, ask the clinic what papers to carry, call my sister Farida so we share the waiting. Things I cannot do: decide what the report says. I read that last line twice, and my chest loosened, like a knot given a little slack. Then I caught myself opening the search page again, and I closed the laptop instead. Dinner was dal and rice, eaten sitting down, the first proper meal today. Whatever Thursday brings, I will not be carrying it alone.
Mohit

qa.q: What did Mohit write on the back of the envelope?
qa.a: Two lists: things Mohit can do, such as booking the driver for Thursday and calling Farida, and things Mohit cannot do, such as deciding what the report says.

qa.q: What did Mohit feel after reading the last line of the lists twice?
qa.a: A little relief. The chest loosened like a knot given slack, so the worry felt lighter even though the results were still to come.

qa.q: Which choice helped Mohit turn worry into something manageable?
qa.a: Mohit split the worry into tasks that were possible and stopped trying to control the report itself, then shared the waiting with Farida instead of holding it alone.

qa.q: How might Farida feel about being called?
qa.a: Farida may feel trusted and glad to share the waiting, since Mohit asked to split it rather than carry it alone.

grounding: A worried adult child does what is possible, releases what is not in their hands, and feels the worry ease.

passage:
Nitin: you still up? demo is at ten tomorrow

qa.q: What is Parul rechecking late at night?
qa.a: Slide 14, for the fifth time.

qa.q: What is Parul worried about, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Parul worries whether the audience will like the demo; the fifth recheck of a finished slide and the joke about it show the anxiety about something outside Parul's control.

qa.q: What could Parul do to stop the worry from taking over the evening?
qa.a: Parul could do what Nitin suggested: accept that the tested work is done, close the laptop and make tea, leaving the audience's reaction alone.

qa.q: How might Nitin see Parul's late-night rechecking?
qa.a: As an understandable worry about something outside Parul's control, which is why Nitin asks what is left, says Parul did the part that is Parul's, and jokes about the tea photo.

grounding: A person worried about a project's outcome sees they have done their part and releases the rest.

subtype: Confusing letting go with giving up [Observer]
passage: My name is Sharmila. Last winter my friend Noor said over chai, "I've let go of him, honestly. I'm fine." Her voice was bright and quick, and in the same breath she asked about my sister's wedding. I nodded. But when I mentioned the café where they used to meet, her jaw tightened and she checked her phone twice. Later, when someone joked about exes, she left the room to take a call that nobody had made. I had always thought letting go would look calm. Noor looked like a person holding a door shut with her shoulder. I didn't argue. A week later I said, "When you want to talk about it, or not, I'm here either way." She looked at the floor and said, "Okay. Maybe soon." I still don't know what she felt, but I stopped calling it peace.

qa.q: What did Noor say over chai?
qa.a: Noor said, "I've let go of him, honestly. I'm fine."

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when Noor left the room to take a call nobody had made?
qa.a: Worried and unsure. Sharmila had expected letting go to look calm, and Noor looked tense, so Sharmila stopped calling it peace.

qa.q: What did Sharmila choose to say instead of arguing that Noor had not let go?
qa.a: Sharmila offered to be there whenever Noor wanted to talk, or not, which left room without pushing.

qa.q: How might Noor feel hearing "I'm here either way"?
qa.a: Noor may feel relieved and less pressured, which fits the quiet "Okay. Maybe soon." It is a cue, not proof of what Noor feels.

grounding: A friend hears 'I have let go' from someone who is still tense and avoiding the topic, and does not mistake that for calm.

subtype: Confusing letting go with giving up [Observer]
passage:
Note, Friday. Vikas, team lead.
Sudha, a friend since our first jobs, told me at lunch, "I've let go of the promotion thing. Totally over it." She said it fast, then asked whether I had seen the new cafeteria menu. Since then I have noticed a few things. She skips any meeting where the new manager presents. Her replies to his emails are one word long. Yesterday when a colleague congratulated him, she went very quiet and stacked the same three folders twice. On days when Sudha really is calm, she laughs and mentions such things herself.
What I did: I did not press. I said, "Whenever you want to talk about it, I'll make the tea." She said thanks, tightly.
Next: check in again next week. If the tension keeps going, I will mention the counsellor.

qa.q: What did Sudha say at lunch?
qa.a: "I've let go of the promotion thing. Totally over it."

qa.q: What was Vikas worried about after watching Sudha stack the same folders twice?
qa.a: Vikas worried that Sudha was still hurting and avoiding the subject rather than being at peace.

qa.q: What did Vikas choose to do instead of pressing Sudha to talk?
qa.a: Vikas offered tea whenever Sudha wanted to talk, and planned to check in next week and mention the counsellor if the tension keeps going.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel when Vikas says "I'll make the tea"?
qa.a: Sudha may feel cared for but still guarded; the tight thanks suggests Sudha is not ready to talk yet.

grounding: A friend notices that someone who says 'I have let go' is still tense and avoiding, and responds gently without assuming.

passage:
Tenzin sat in the high chair, banging a spoon on the tray.
"Ba-ba-ba!" Then Tenzin stopped and looked at Mama Sharmila, mouth open, waiting.
"Ba-ba? Is that so?" said Sharmila.
Tenzin grinned. "Da! Ba-da-da." Pause. Eyes on Mama's face.
"Da-da-da! You are telling me a story."
"Bah!" Tenzin slapped the tray, laughed, and waited again.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do after saying "Ba-ba-ba!"?
qa.a: Tenzin stopped and looked at Sharmila, mouth open, waiting.

qa.q: What does Tenzin's waiting, with eyes on Mama's face, suggest Tenzin wants?
qa.a: An answer. The pause and the steady look show Tenzin expects a reply and enjoys getting one.

qa.q: What could Sharmila do to keep the exchange going?
qa.a: Answer each sound in a warm voice and then wait for the next one, as Sharmila did by saying "You are telling me a story."

qa.q: What is it like for Sharmila when Tenzin pauses and looks up?
qa.a: Sharmila is invited to take a turn. The pause shows it is time to reply, and each reply gets Tenzin laughing and babbling again.

grounding: A toddler babbles, pauses and waits for Mama to reply, then babbles again.

passage:
Daily note from the crèche, Ramesh.
Shankar sat by the window with the toy phone and said, "Hallo? Hallo?" Then Shankar tilted the head, waiting. I said, "Hello! Where are you going?" Shankar said, "Bus!" and paused again. I replied, "The bus goes to the market." Shankar giggled, babbled a string of sounds, and waited. We went back and forth until snack time.
Next: I told Shankar's grandmother that bath time can be the same. Answer each sound, then wait.

qa.q: What did Shankar say into the toy phone?
qa.a: "Hallo? Hallo?"

qa.q: What might Shankar be expecting when pausing after saying "Bus!"?
qa.a: A reply from Ramesh. The tilted head and the waiting show Shankar expects the other person to take a turn, and the giggling shows delight when it comes.

qa.q: What simple habit does Ramesh suggest for home?
qa.a: To answer each sound Shankar makes and then wait, during ordinary times like bath time and meals.

qa.q: How might Ramesh's note help Shankar's grandmother?
qa.a: It shows that no special lessons are needed: answering each sound and waiting is already the kind of conversation that helps Shankar.

grounding: A toddler babbles, pauses and waits for a caregiver to answer, and the exchange repeats.

passage: I am Yamini, the neighbour upstairs. On Sunday I was on Rafiq's balcony, telling Rafiq's papa about the water tank repair, when Rafiq burst in: "Papa, Papa, a red bus, I saw a red bus!" Papa held up one finger and said, "Two minutes, dost, then it's your turn." Rafiq's mouth stayed open, feet danced on the tiles, and one hand pressed against the lips. When the tank story ended, Papa turned right away: "Now. The red bus?" Rafiq shouted the whole story in one breath.

qa.q: What did Rafiq say when bursting in?
qa.a: "Papa, Papa, a red bus, I saw a red bus!"

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling while waiting for the two minutes?
qa.a: Impatient and perhaps afraid the thought would vanish. The dancing feet and the hand pressed on the lips show a hard struggle to wait.

qa.q: What worked better than scolding in this scene?
qa.a: Papa's one raised finger and a promise of a turn in two minutes, followed by really giving that turn.

qa.q: What might Papa be feeling when holding up a finger instead of scolding?
qa.a: Patient and calm, wanting to respect the talk with Yamini and Rafiq's excitement at once.

grounding: A child interrupts an adult's conversation because the thought might vanish, and a signal plus a promised turn helps.

passage:
Monday: At school story time, Usha shouted, "My cat did that too!" in the middle of Ms Parveen's sentence, and again two lines later. Ms Parveen said, "Usha, please wait." Usha's shoulders dropped.
Wednesday: Ms Parveen knelt by Usha's chair. "When a thought pops up, put your hand flat on your chest. I will see it, and you get the next turn." They practised twice.
Friday: In a rainy-day story, Usha's hand went flat on the chest, cheeks puffed with waiting. Ms Parveen nodded, finished the page, and said, "Now, Usha, your cat?" Usha talked for a whole minute.

qa.q: What hand signal did Ms Parveen teach Usha?
qa.a: Putting a hand flat on the chest when a thought pops up.

qa.q: What might Usha have felt after hearing "please wait" on Monday?
qa.a: Discouraged, maybe a bit embarrassed. The dropped shoulders show the wish to share had been dampened.

qa.q: What turning point on Wednesday helped Usha wait?
qa.a: Ms Parveen knelt down, taught the hand-on-chest signal and promised the next turn, then practised it twice.

qa.q: What is it like for Ms Parveen on Friday to see Usha's hand on the chest?
qa.a: Encouraging. It shows the signal works and Usha is practising waiting, and Ms Parveen keeps the promise by finishing the page and then turning to Usha.

grounding: A child who blurts out learns to wait through a hand signal and a promised turn, over three days.

passage:
Club diary, Vinita, teacher-in-charge of the film club.
At Thursday's meeting Urmila spoke for most of the hour: the short-film idea, her cousin's camera, a trip to the coast. She did not ask anyone a question. I watched the others. Faiz began drawing in the margin of a notebook. Two students checked their phones under the table. Meera, who had brought three story ideas last month, stopped offering any. Urmila did not seem to notice at all.
I did not call Urmila out in front of the group. After the meeting I asked, "Which of the others' ideas stayed with you today?" Urmila paused for a long moment. Next week I will try a round where each person speaks for one minute.

qa.q: Who stopped offering story ideas at the Thursday meeting?
qa.a: Meera, who had brought three story ideas the month before.

qa.q: What was Vinita worried about while watching the group?
qa.a: That the quieter members were disengaging quietly, while Urmila seemed not to notice.

qa.q: What did Vinita choose to do instead of calling Urmila out in front of the group?
qa.a: Vinita asked Urmila privately which of the others' ideas had stayed with Urmila, and planned a one-minute round for next week.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel when asked which of the others' ideas stayed with her?
qa.a: Possibly surprised or a little embarrassed, then thoughtful. The long pause suggests Urmila had not been listening for the others' ideas and began to notice.

grounding: A group notices one member who takes the floor and rarely asks anything back, while others quietly disengage.

passage:
Saturday night. Lunch with my friends again, and Payal did nearly all the talking, first about her cousin's wedding photographs, then about her exam predictions. She never asked Tanya a single thing back. I watched. Tanya turned the water bottle around and around. Ishaan started scrolling. I opened my mouth twice and closed it twice. I like Payal, she's funny and generous, and I'm pretty sure she has no idea. I don't know what to do. Maybe next time I'll ask Tanya a small question in a gap, like "Did you finish the sketch?", and see whether Payal follows. If it keeps happening, maybe I'll tell Payal kindly, when it's just the two of us.
Mahima

qa.q: What did Tanya do while Payal talked?
qa.a: Tanya turned the water bottle around and around.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling about speaking up at lunch?
qa.a: Torn and unsure. Mahima likes Payal and wants to include Tanya, but opened and closed the mouth twice without speaking.

qa.q: What small step does Mahima plan to try next time?
qa.a: To ask Tanya a small question in a gap, like whether the sketch is finished, and see whether Payal follows.

qa.q: How might Payal see the lunch?
qa.a: Probably as an enjoyable chat. Mahima is pretty sure Payal has no idea the others are losing interest.

grounding: A friend notices one person always takes the floor, others disengage, and the dominant person is unaware.

passage:
Monday: Four friends argued about the route for the hostel trip, and Uday sat at the end of the bench peeling the label off a bottle. Deepak noticed, and said nothing yet.
Wednesday: While the others argued, Deepak leaned over. "Uday, what do you think? No pressure, pass is fine too." Uday hesitated. "The night bus loses a whole day. The lake stop is better on the way back." The others paused. "Huh, that's actually smart," said Meghna.
Saturday: Uday sent a short plan to the group chat. Deepak was first to reply: "Booked it the way Uday said." Meghna sent three thumbs up, and Uday sent back a photo of the lake.

qa.q: What was Uday doing at the end of the bench on Monday?
qa.a: Peeling the label off a bottle.

qa.q: What might Uday have been feeling while sitting at the end of the bench?
qa.a: Left out or unsure about speaking. Uday stayed quiet and fiddled with the label while the others argued.

qa.q: What made Deepak's question easy for Uday to answer?
qa.a: Deepak asked what Uday thought and added "No pressure, pass is fine too," so Uday could say yes or no without being cornered.

qa.q: What is it like for the others when Uday speaks up?
qa.a: They are surprised and interested. They pause, and Meghna says it is actually smart, so the plan improves.

grounding: A young adult asks a quiet friend what they think without pressure, and the group's plan becomes richer.

passage:
Kiran, sit. Let me tell you about my second year in the hostel. Five of us prepared for the exam around one table, and the talk belonged to the loud ones. Lata sat with her notebook closed, and I saw her pen tapping. I could have carried on with my own point. Instead I turned and said, "Lata, what do you think? Only if you want to." Lata blinked. Then, slowly, she said the problem we had been stuck on could be solved the other way round. Nobody spoke for a moment. That night the table felt wider. Lata says even now that it was the first time anyone had waited for her.
Kavitha

qa.q: How many people studied around the table?
qa.a: Five, including Kavitha.

qa.q: What was Kavitha thinking when watching Lata's pen tapping?
qa.a: That Lata had something to say but was not being given a gap to say it.

qa.q: What choice did Kavitha make that changed the evening?
qa.a: Kavitha set aside the point Kavitha was making and asked Lata, "What do you think? Only if you want to."

qa.q: How might Lata have felt when the whole table waited for the answer?
qa.a: Heard and valued, maybe a little nervous at first, since Lata blinked before answering slowly.

grounding: An older person recalls asking a quiet member of the study group for a view, opening a turn without pressure.

passage:
"And that's why the vendor plan stays," said the director, moving straight to the next slide.
Shreya waited for a gap. There was none. Beside Shreya, Suraj whispered, "They never stop for breath."
"Four long stretches so far, and nobody under senior has spoken," Shreya whispered back. "Watch." Then, aloud, at the next comma: "Sir, may I take one minute on the vendor timing? It affects the March launch."
The director paused. "Go ahead."
Afterwards in the corridor Suraj said, "How did you dare?"
"I asked for a minute, not the floor," said Shreya. "My hands were shaking, though."

qa.q: What did Shreya ask the director at the next comma?
qa.a: For one minute on the vendor timing, because it affects the March launch.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling after asking, according to the corridor talk?
qa.a: Nervous. Shreya said the hands were shaking, even though the request sounded calm.

qa.q: What wording made the request easy for the director to grant?
qa.a: Asking for one minute, not the floor, and giving a reason tied to the March launch.

qa.q: How might the director see Shreya's request?
qa.a: As reasonable and useful, since the director paused and said "Go ahead"; the director may not have realised the juniors could find no gap.

grounding: A young employee sees juniors wait for gaps in a meeting and shows that asking the chair for a minute works.

passage: My name is Zainab. In my first quarter at a logistics company, the weekly review was mostly one person talking. Joseph, the senior manager, would speak in long stretches, and the juniors waited for gaps that never came. I watched it for three weeks. Divya tapped a pen. Others looked at the clock. Nobody was being rude; the room simply ran that way. So I practised. I wrote a sentence in my notebook, and at the end of a topic I said, "Joseph, could I add one point before we move on?" My voice cracked the first time. He said, "Of course," and listened. Since then I've treated it as a skill: name the gap, ask for a minute, keep it short.

qa.q: How long did Zainab watch the pattern in the weekly review before acting?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling the first time of asking for a point, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Nervous. The voice cracked the first time, even though the request was short and polite.

qa.q: What did Zainab do to prepare before speaking up in the review?
qa.a: Zainab wrote a sentence in a notebook and waited for the end of a topic to ask, "Joseph, could I add one point before we move on?"

qa.q: How might Joseph see the juniors' silence in the review?
qa.a: Joseph may not realise that the juniors are waiting for a gap; Joseph said "Of course" and listened once asked.

grounding: A young employee sees seniors talk in long stretches, learns to name a gap, and asks the chair for a minute.

passage:
Monday: Joseph was stacking blocks into a tall tower when Joseph's mama, Aparna, called from the kitchen, "Shoes on, please!" Joseph kept stacking. The bus was missed.
Tuesday: Aparna walked over, crouched to eye level, and said, "Joseph." Joseph looked up. "Shoes on, please." Joseph fetched them right away.
Wednesday: Joseph was rolling a toy train along the sofa. Aparna crouched beside it and said, "Joseph." The train stopped. "Shoes?" said Joseph, and ran to the door.

qa.q: What was Joseph doing on Monday when Aparna called from the kitchen?
qa.a: Stacking blocks into a tall tower.

qa.q: What was Joseph's mind on when Aparna called from the kitchen?
qa.a: The tower of blocks. Joseph heard the sound but was absorbed and did not take in the words.

qa.q: What change did Aparna make on Tuesday that helped?
qa.a: Aparna walked over, crouched to eye level and said Joseph's name first, then gave the instruction.

qa.q: How might Aparna have felt on Monday when the bus was missed?
qa.a: Frustrated and hurried, perhaps thinking Joseph was ignoring the call, when Joseph had not really taken it in.

grounding: A child hears Mama's instruction while absorbed in play and does not process it; eye level and a name call help.

passage: The railway platform was loud with announcements and rolling suitcases. Chetan stood watching pigeons peck at crumbs near the yellow line, right in front of a waiting bag trolley. Chetan's mum, Simran, called out, "Chetan, hold my hand!" once, then again. Chetan did not turn; the pigeons were the whole world. A train horn sounded in the distance. Simran stepped over, crouched, touched Chetan's shoulder and said, "Chetan." Chetan's eyes came round. "Look at me. Hold my hand, the train is coming." Chetan's small hand slipped into Simran's, and they moved back from the yellow line together.

qa.q: What was Chetan watching on the platform?
qa.a: Pigeons pecking at crumbs near the yellow line.

qa.q: What was on Chetan's mind when Simran called out?
qa.a: The pigeons. Chetan heard the noise but was completely absorbed, so the words did not sink in.

qa.q: What did Simran change that finally worked?
qa.a: Simran stepped over, crouched, touched Chetan's shoulder and said the name, then gave a short instruction once Chetan looked.

qa.q: How might Simran have felt when the train horn sounded and Chetan did not turn?
qa.a: Worried and hurried, since the noise was loud, Chetan was near the yellow line, and calling from a distance was not working.

grounding: A child hears Mum's instruction while looking at something else and does not process it; eye level and a name call help, even in a noisy place.

passage:
Chidi and Anders were sitting on the cold steps behind the school in Malmö. "The ball went into the pond yesterday," said Chidi. "Someone said it was you."
"It wasn't me!" said Anders. "It was Emil, I told him not to kick it that hard. And I wasn't even there when—"
"I know," said Chidi. "I was going to say the caretaker got it out with a net, and it's fine."
Anders stopped. "Oh." The ears went pink. "I thought you were saying it was my fault."
"You didn't let me finish," said Chidi, half laughing.
"Sorry," said Anders. "So the ball is fine?"

qa.q: Where did Chidi and Anders sit while they talked?
qa.a: On the cold steps behind the school in Malmö.

qa.q: What was Anders worried about when Chidi mentioned the pond?
qa.a: Being blamed. Anders rushed to defend and said it was Emil, without waiting to hear what Chidi meant.

qa.q: What could Anders try next time when someone brings up something like this?
qa.a: Wait until Chidi finishes and ask, "What do you mean?" before answering, so that nothing gets defended that was never an accusation.

qa.q: What is it like for Chidi to be cut off?
qa.a: Chidi wanted to share good news about the ball and could not get to it, which is a little funny but also frustrating, since it shows Anders was not hearing the whole thing.

grounding: A child listens only enough to defend, and misses what the other person is actually saying.

passage:
In the reading corner at school, Tenzin was telling a small group about the mela. "There was a big wheel that went so high, and we ate hot jalebi, and the—"
"Actually, it was Sunday," said Imran. "You said Saturday before."
Tenzin stopped. "Oh. Sunday." The story trailed off.
Imran folded both arms, looking pleased to have caught the slip. The teacher, sitting nearby, said, "Imran, what was the best part of Tenzin's story so far?"
Imran opened the mouth. "Um... it was Sunday."
"That's a good detail," said the teacher gently. "What about the wheel?"
Imran looked at the floor. "I didn't hear about the wheel."

qa.q: What day did Imran say the mela was on?
qa.a: Sunday.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when catching Tenzin's slip, and what does that suggest?
qa.a: Pleased with catching a mistake. The folded arms and the pleased look suggest Imran was listening for errors, not for the story.

qa.q: How could the teacher help Imran listen differently?
qa.a: The teacher asked what the best part of the story was so far, which pointed Imran toward the meaning rather than the mistake; a next step could be asking Tenzin one question about the wheel.

qa.q: How does Tenzin feel when the story is stopped by a correction?
qa.a: Deflated. The story trailed off after the correction, so Tenzin's excitement about the mela was lost.

grounding: A child listens only in order to correct, so the storyteller loses the thread and the listener misses the story.

passage:
Kiran sat on the colony terrace after dinner, picking at a loose thread on the cushion. Bhupen, a friend from the next building, had come up to return a notebook, phone in hand, scrolling.
"Can I tell you something?" said Kiran. "I keep lying awake thinking I'll blank on the chemistry paper. Everyone else seems fine."
Bhupen looked up. Then Bhupen turned the phone face down on the step and said, "Blank how? Like the whole paper, or one question that throws you off?"
Kiran hadn't expected that. Words came slowly at first, then all together. Bhupen didn't give a list of tips. Bhupen just nodded and asked, "And then what happens in your head?"
When Kiran got to the stairs, the shoulders felt lighter.

qa.q: Where was Kiran sitting when telling Bhupen about the worry?
qa.a: On the colony terrace after dinner, picking at a loose thread on the cushion.

qa.q: What did Kiran feel when Bhupen put the phone face down and asked a follow-up?
qa.a: Surprise, then relief. The words came slowly and then all together, and the shoulders felt lighter afterwards.

qa.q: What did Bhupen choose to do that made the difference?
qa.a: Bhupen turned the phone face down and asked a follow-up question instead of handing over a list of tips.

qa.q: What might Bhupen have been thinking when Kiran said, "Can I tell you something?"
qa.a: That Kiran wanted to be listened to, not fixed, which is why Bhupen put the phone away and asked what happens in the head.

grounding: A teenager tells a friend a worry, and the friend puts the phone down and asks a follow-up, so the teenager feels heard.

passage:
"Can I tell you something?" Dhruv said, sitting down on the bench by the bus stop next to Shalini, a friend since Class Five.
"Sure." Shalini was texting, but quickly slid the phone into a pocket. "Go on."
"I'm scared I'll freeze at the audition for the school play. My hands go cold even thinking about it."
"Cold hands. Wait, is it the first line that scares you most?"
"Yeah. Just the first line. After that I think I'd be okay."
"Then that's a really specific thing. Tell me more about the first line."
Dhruv laughed shakily. "You didn't tell me what to do."
"Did you want me to?"
"No. I wanted you to ask that." Dhruv leaned back. "Thanks for the pocket thing."

qa.q: What is Dhruv scared of?
qa.a: Freezing at the audition for the school play, especially on the first line.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when saying "Thanks for the pocket thing"?
qa.a: Grateful and relieved. Dhruv noticed Shalini put the phone away and felt that mattered more than advice.

qa.q: What did Shalini do that made Dhruv feel heard?
qa.a: Shalini slid the phone into a pocket, asked a follow-up about the first line, and did not offer advice unless it was wanted.

qa.q: What is it like for Shalini to hear "You didn't tell me what to do"?
qa.a: It may be a small surprise. Shalini can see that listening and asking counted for more than solutions, so asking "Did you want me to?" was the right move.

grounding: A teenager tells a friend a worry, sees the friend put the phone away and ask a follow-up, and feels heard more than advised.
